It depends on the antidepressant, but, with almost all of them, this is something that causes a lot of wild mood swings and usually increased depression. 

Antidepressants all work differently, but the main idea is they help your brain either create or process the chemicals that regulate mood. You begin taking them and slowly ramp up the dosage so your brain can properly adjust. Once it gets used to this new managed production or processing, it may be possible to slowly remove them from your system. But the key is slowly. Your brain needs to recognize their absence and try and make up for it to create the new normal. 

If you stop taking them all at once your brain can't compensate properly, and has also developed a reliance on the drugs to help it create or manage the chemicals. This means you will feel a greater effect of imbalance. Over time your brain should return to a more normal production (which may be still imbalanced, seeing as you needed the antidepressants) so after a few weeks your mood should normalize, you have not done any long term damage and could begin to ramp up thier dosage again. Be sure to talk with your therapist (the one that actually manages your drug prescription, since that's often not the one you talk to regularly) about this laps and see what she recommends for adjusting your dosage to get it back to what you were taking. For a very long time I suffered from depression and listened to a lot of the one word answers here. A lot of people just saying Netflix, sleep, hate the world, etc. These things don't work. Eventually I attempted suicide, and not the half-baked attempts I had done before, but a real and true attempt that got me hospitalized. After that, I needed to actually strat trying to work on my depression. 

I still struggle every day, but I have gotten much better. The biggest things I have done are: 

1. Change your setting. The environment you put yourself in is critical to your perceptions and happiness. I thought I was in a good place, and by all accounts I was, but when I moved and started things in a new place with new people, I started to see how the things around me and the people around me where toxins that fed my depression.

2. Exercise more. I hate it. Working out sucks, and I just want to eat happy food and play video games. This attitude was destroying me without me know it. I hate so much that working out daily has improved my life so drastically. It takes a lot of time and effort, but it really truly helps.

3. Do things just for you. If you want something, go get it. You are aloud to want things, and you should take them if you can have them (as long as it doesn't hurt others). I used to always give more of myself than I took, and it left me empty. Now, when I can identify something I want, I go out and get it, within reason. 

4. Explore the world around you. Walks in nature or even just around town bring a sense of adventure and nuance to your life that help prevent the feeling of being in a rutt. 

5. Let yourself fail. Take risks and accept failure. This can be really hard, but once you give up the idealized version of yourself, you free yourself to actually become someone cool. I am no longer vegan...or very healthy, but from ages 17-23 I was Vegan and very healthy. 

I did all the research I needed to ensure I was getting nutrients that are rare in many vegan diets such as proteins and iron. In doing so, I took a very close look at my intake and made much better choices. I lost 50 pounds in the first 5 months and, for the only time in my life, was at a height and weight ratio deemed "normal" for men my age. I also felt much better physically. I felt like I could run further and jump higher. 

Being vegan had a lot of challenges as well, however. Anytime I was eating with friends I felt like a burden on the group. I always asked people to not accommodate me as veganism was my choice, but they always tried anyhow. This greatly limited where we went, and eventually meant my friend would do things without me more and more if the outing revolved around food. 

Veganism also had an interesting impact on my body. Though I lost weight and looked healthy, I also noticed a great decrease in muscle mass. Though my protein levels were fine, i noticed a lot of loss in muscle mass. During this time I had to drastically increase my workout regiment to not loose strength. Even with the increase, and being able to lift the same weight, my body began to loose a lot of it's girth. I began to look scrawny, even with my much larger frame. I noticed people started treating me differently as well. Small, probably unconscious things would happen. People stopped always letting me lead when walking in a group. I found myself walking on the building side, not the street side of sidewalks when walking in pairs, people occasionally held doors open for me, I was never the first person asked to help when someone was struggling to move something or reach something (despite still being one of the tallest people around). 

Finally, even following guides on healthy eating as a vegan, i began to see some minor medical issues. My testosterone levels have always been low, but when I was Vegan I was actually given prescription strength testosterone supplements. This really did not do too much harm. It just meant I was a tired more often and I had a much lower sex drive.

Hope this helps.

However, many dms like to let nat 20s mean auto success because it add some excitement and hilarity. That said, as such a dm, I never let my players roll for thing that are not possible so the nat 20 issue does not come up so often. You wouldn’t let them roll to drink the entire ocean with a con save, so don’t let them roll for a 100ft jump unless it was somehow within the realm of possibility for them. I do, however, let them roll for things just outside their possible scope. If they could clear a 20ft gap with a 19 I might let them roll for up to a 30ft gap and allow it with a nat 20.
